title: The investigation of type and concentration of bio-aerosols in the air of surgical rooms: A case study in Shariati hospital, Karaj
author: Tolabi, Alimohammadi, et al.

steps.title: Prepare culture plates
steps.instruction: Prepare Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) plates for fungi and add cycloheximide to a final concentration of 500 mg L⁻¹; prepare tryptic soy agar (TSA) plates for bacteria and add chloramphenicol to a final concentration of 100 mg L⁻¹. Pour each medium into 9‑cm‑diameter Petri dishes, allow to solidify, and keep lids open until sampling.

substeps.instruction: SDA + cycloheximide (500 mg L⁻¹) for fungal sampling
TSA + chloramphenicol (100 mg L⁻¹) for bacterial sampling

steps.title: Label and package plates
steps.instruction: Label each 9‑cm plate with operating‑room name, sampling point, date, and target organism (bacterial or fungal). Place each labeled plate in a zip‑lock bag and store the bags in a cool box until transport to the operating rooms.

steps.title: Define sampling layout and schedule
steps.instruction: Identify the four operating rooms (orthopedic, eye, cesarean, internal). In the internal surgical room select two sampling points; in the other rooms select three points (entrance, near surgical bed, end of room). Plan six sampling stages over the 180‑day study period (May 2016 – Feb 2017), with each stage collecting samples before surgery, during surgery, and after surgery. Record the surgical incision size for every sampling event.

steps.title: Deploy passive settle plates
steps.instruction: At each sampling point, place a 9‑cm plate on a stool so that the agar surface is 1 m above the floor and at least 1 m away from walls, windows, doors, or any obstacles (standard 1/1/1 passive sampling method). Open the plate lid and expose the agar to ambient air for exactly 1 h. After 1 h, close the lid.

steps.title: Retrieve and transport plates
steps.instruction: After the 1‑hour exposure, close the lids, note the sampling time and the recorded incision size, place each plate back into its zip‑lock bag, and transport all plates to the Microbiology Laboratory of Shariati Hospital in a cool box.

steps.title: Document sample totals
steps.instruction: Over the 180‑day period, a total of 198 bacterial and 198 fungal samples are collected according to the schedule.

description: Aerosols are among important air pollutants producing due to natural processes and human activities [1,2]. Human exposure to bioaerosols in indoor air causes many problems in health care centers. High concentrations of different bioaerosols species are reported in hospitals. Exposure to bioaerosols is associated with adverse health effects, including transmission of infectious diseases, acute toxic effects, and respiratory syndromes such as asthma and allergies [3]. The presence of bioaerosols in the hospital wards is one of the main causes of hospital infections and can be dangerous especially for immunocompromised patients [4]. Overall, hospital infections impose important health and economic problems on societies, with an estimated population of around 1.4 million people being affected at any given moment in the world [5]. Bioaerosols are contaminant particles that contain microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi spores and their related products (endotoxin, mycotoxin, etc.), viruses, pollen grains, fungi, plant residues, insect fragments, and human and animal skin cells [[6], [7], [8], [9]]. The bio-aerosol particles range from 0.001–100 μm in diameter [10]. Bioaerosols smaller than ten μm in diameter create more severe health complications, especially in hospitals [11]. Previous studies have attributed about 5–34% of indoor air contamination to the presence of bioaerosols. Respiratory symptoms and decreased lung function are one of the most critical health complications of exposure to bioaerosols [12]. Bacteria and fungi make up a wide range of microorganisms that enter the hospital indoor air through ventilation systems, visitors and patients [13,14]. Passive sampling is arguably the most readily available, economical, and unobtrusive method of bioaerosol sampling and relies on particles settling using gravity, on a collection substrate housed in a settle plate [15].
